reviewerDerivedProposition: An effective escalation states the concern plainly, supplies the relevant background, presents objective TRENDS rather than isolated values, and closes with a specific request. Here the urgent message is not fever or confusion in isolation but a trajectory consistent with bleeding and hypoperfusion: deteriorating vital signs from 0700 to 1100, a change in mental status, falling urine output, increasing and darkening drain output, and an expanding dressing stain. The nurse asks for bedside assessment now. Framing the abnormal findings as ordinary postoperative changes, or requesting only an antipyretic and waiting for rounds, defeats the purpose of the call.
requiredFacts: The 0700 baseline values that make a trend readable - baseline_0700 global exhibit.

The 0900 and 1100 deterioration - lightheadedness, HR to 102, BP to 112/68, intermittent confusion, urine output falling to 20 mL/hr, drain output increasing and turning frankly sanguineous, dressing stain expanding to 6 cm - stage_1_0900_1100.
Nothing from stage_2 or stage_3 is required. I checked each keyed option against the stage_1 prefix and all four are fully supported there.
disclosureEvidence: Hiding stage_2 is ESSENTIAL and is what makes this row work. stage_2 opens: 'The nurse prepares to call the surgical resident using SBAR, organizing the vital-sign trend, mental-status change, declining urine output, increasing and darkening drain output, expanding dressing stain, and fever trend.' That enumeration is keyed options C and D almost word for word. stage_2 further supplies both distractors, since the resident's reply that 'some confusion and low-grade fever can occur postoperatively' is distractor B and the recommendation of acetaminophen with a check at afternoon rounds is distractor F - so with stage_2 visible a learner could identify the distractors as the inadequate response being criticised. At the stage_1 boundary none of this is visible and the item becomes a genuine judgement task. stage_3 confirms the haemorrhage and must also be hidden.
clinicalVerdict: Correct. The keyed set covers all four SBAR elements with the right emphasis, and option C carries the item's real teaching point - that a trend communicates deterioration where a single set of values does not. Option E is carefully worded, requesting bedside assessment while discussing diagnostics and interventions 'appropriate to the provider's scope', which keeps the nurse inside her own scope rather than prescribing. Both distractors are genuine and instructive errors rather than filler: B is the minimisation that the case goes on to dramatise, and F is the deferral that leads to the chain-of-command escalation. The option set contains four correct options and two real errors, so discrimination is sound. I found no invented fact, no stranded value and no key ambiguity.
contentDefects: NONE REQUIRING REPAIR. One MEDIUM-confidence observation offered as a recommendation: the stem is prefixed 'Stage 2:' in both languages while the anchor places the learner at Stage 1, so the label points at a stage the renderer is withholding. The stem is otherwise entirely self-carrying - it asks what the nurse SHOULD include in an upcoming call - and nothing in the option set is stranded by the boundary, so unlike the comparable case in the lithium parent this label does not break the item. I recommend the prefix be adjusted to refer to the impending call rather than to Stage 2, but I do not treat it as blocking.
bilingualVerdict: PARALLEL - I read the Chinese against the English for the stem, all six options and all six byChoice rationales. Each pair is semantically equivalent, including the trend emphasis in option C and the scope qualifier in option E. The 'Stage 2' prefix appears in Chinese as '阶段 2：' and carries the same label issue in both languages.
sourcesChecked: No external premise was load-bearing. The SBAR structure and the principle that trends communicate deterioration better than isolated values are standard escalation practice and are not in dispute; the item's correctness turns on whether each keyed element is supported by the visible prefix, which I verified option by option against the baseline and stage_1 exhibits.
siblingImpact: NONE. This is an anchor-only repair; no learner-facing text changes. I note that sibling q2 already carries a resolving stage_1_0900_1100 anchor, so this row's boundary is consistent with an accepted sibling in the same parent.
repairConstraints: Set answerableAfterStageId to stage_1_0900_1100. No content change is required or authorised by this row.

Do NOT anchor at stage_2, which would disclose keyed options C and D and both distractors, and do not anchor at baseline, where the 0900 and 1100 deterioration that the whole call concerns does not yet exist.
Consider the stem-prefix adjustment noted above as optional follow-up, not as part of this repair.
criticalNote: This is the clearest case in the population of an anchor doing real remedial work through a NON-terminal boundary. The producer's proposal places the learner one stage before the stage that enumerates the answer, and the item survives intact there. It is worth contrasting with the several rows where the correct boundary is terminal and the anchor therefore changes nothing.
agreementReasoning: I independently found the stage_2 enumeration that would disclose options C and D, and independently verified that all four keyed options are supported at stage_1, which is what makes the earlier boundary viable rather than merely convenient. Codex reached the same boundary with no content work and its reasoning about what stage_2 and stage_3 would reveal is accurate. I tested the no-defect claim by checking each option against the visible prefix, checking for the all-correct degeneracy found elsewhere, examining the title and summary for the diagnostic-leak pattern, and reading the Chinese in full. I add the dangling stage-label observation as a recommendation. The Campaign-16 producer's stage_1 was correct and the checker's baseline was too early.
